sources.fact: Brain freeze is a brief, intense pain in the front of the head; scientific term sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia; usually lasts a few seconds to two minutes; not serious; talk to a provider about frequent headaches that last a while
Swinburne University physiologists (The Conversation): the brain can't sense cold or pain because it lacks its own internal sensory receptors; cold over the hard palate can trigger brain freeze

Virginia Tech Carilion neuroscientist Kristofer Rau: cold prompts a rapid increase of warm blood flow through vessels in the roof of the mouth; the sudden expansion is sensed by nerve cells and interpreted as pain; goes away within seconds to a minute or so

math.note: Cleveland Clinic: a few seconds to two minutes

post.instagram_caption:
Brain freeze has a real scientific name, and it's a mouthful 🍦

It's called sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia. Your brain itself has no pain sensors: cold hits the roof of your mouth, blood vessels there quickly widen to warm things up, and nerves report it as pain in the front of your head. It usually lasts a few seconds, up to two minutes. If you get frequent headaches that last a while, see a doctor.

Your brain isn't freezing. It's just hearing the complaints.

Sources: Cleveland Clinic, Swinburne University, Virginia Tech.
